title: Testing primaryness of a homogeneous ideal on homogeneous factors
statement: Let $R=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}R_d$ be a commutative ring graded by the nonnegative integers: every element has a unique finite decomposition into elements of the additive subgroups $R_d$, $1\in R_0$, and $R_aR_b\subseteq R_{a+b}$. Assume $R$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Let $J\subsetneq R$ be a homogeneous ideal, meaning that each homogeneous component of every element of $J$ lies in $J$. An element is homogeneous if it belongs to some $R_d$. Suppose that for every pair of homogeneous elements $a,b\in R$, if $ab\in J$ and $a\notin J$, then $b^h\in J$ for some integer $h\ge1$. Then $J$ is primary: for arbitrary $u,v\in R$, if $uv\in J$ and $u\notin J$, then $v^n\in J$ for some integer $n\ge1$.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF p.130), specialized to M=R and the proper homogeneous submodule J. nil(R/J)=sqrt(J), since a power annihilates R/J exactly when it sends 1 into J. Local PDF WANTED; authors PDF read online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf.

proof.text: Fix arbitrary $u,v\in R$ with $uv\in J$ and $u\notin J$. Write $u=\sum_i u_i$ and $v=\sum_j v_j$ in their finite homogeneous decompositions, inserting zero components where necessary. Some $u_i$ lies outside $J$, since otherwise their sum would belong to $J$. Let $t$ be the least such degree, set $q=\sum_{i<t}u_i\in J$, and put $w=u-q$. Then $vw=uv-vq\in J$, $w_i=0$ for $i<t$, and $w_t=u_t\notin J$.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF page index 129), specialized to M=R. Local PDF WANTED; read authors PDF online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Lowest-component argument expanded with the correct power.

proof.text: Suppose first that every nonzero component $v_j$ has a positive power in $J$, and choose $e_j\ge1$ with $v_j^{e_j}\in J$ for each such degree. Set $N=1+\sum_j(e_j-1)\ge1$, taking $N=1$ when $v=0$. Expand $v^N=(\sum_j v_j)^N$ by distributivity. Every term is a product of $N$ components; if each $v_j$ occurred at most $e_j-1$ times, it would have at most $N-1$ factors. Thus some $v_j^{e_j}$ divides every term. Every term and hence $v^N$ lies in $J$. This gives the required conclusion in this case.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF page index 129), specialized to M=R. Local PDF WANTED; read authors PDF online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Lowest-component argument expanded with the correct power.

proof.text: It remains to exclude the case where some component has no positive power in $J$. Let $s$ be the least degree with this property and put $c=v_s$. For each nonzero $v_j$ with $j<s$, choose $e_j\ge1$ with $v_j^{e_j}\in J$. Put $a=\sum_{j<s}v_j$ and $k=1+\sum_{j<s,\,v_j\ne0}(e_j-1)\ge1$. The same distributive expansion as in step 2 shows $a^k\in J$; for an empty sum this says $0^1\in J$. Set $z=v-a$. Its components below $s$ vanish and its degree-$s$ component is $c$.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF page index 129), specialized to M=R. Local PDF WANTED; read authors PDF online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Lowest-component argument expanded with the correct power.

proof.text: Expand $(v-a)^k w$. The term with no factor $v$ is $(-a)^k w\in J$, since $a^k\in J$. Every other term contains at least one factor $v$, and therefore is a multiple of $vw\in J$. Additive closure of $J$ gives $z^k w\in J$. This argument uses commutativity to reorder factors; it does not assert that $zw$ itself belongs to $J$.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF page index 129), specialized to M=R. Local PDF WANTED; read authors PDF online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Lowest-component argument expanded with the correct power.

proof.text: In the finite distributive expansion of $z^k w$, each of the $k$ components chosen from $z$ has degree at least $s$, and the component chosen from $w$ has degree at least $t$. Their total degree equals $ks+t$ only when every chosen $z$-degree is $s$ and the chosen $w$-degree is $t$. Hence the degree-$(ks+t)$ component is exactly $c^k u_t$. (This identity still holds when that product is zero.) Since $J$ is homogeneous and $z^k w\in J$, we obtain $c^k u_t\in J$.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, printed p.122 (PDF page index 129), specialized to M=R. Local PDF WANTED; read authors PDF online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Lowest-component argument expanded with the correct power.

proof.text: Both $u_t\in R_t$ and $c^k\in R_{ks}$ are homogeneous, and $u_t\notin J$. Apply the hypothesis of the item to the pair $(u_t,c^k)$, using commutativity and step 5. It yields $(c^k)^h=c^{kh}\in J$ for some $h\ge1$. As $kh\ge1$, this contradicts the defining choice of $s$. The remaining case is impossible, so step 2 always supplies a positive power of $v$ in $J$. As $u,v$ were arbitrary and $J$ is proper, this proves primaryness with exactly the asserted meaning.
